en.title: Music: the whole course
en.short: What music study covers, how music degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Music is both an art and an academic discipline. It studies organised sound: how people make it, hear it, write it down, teach it, perform it, record it and use it in society. Academic music joins practical work (performance, composition, arranging, conducting) with history, theory, analysis, ethnomusicology, psychology, technology, education, business and law. It is not only training for performers. Graduates become teachers, performers, composers, producers, researchers, administrators, music therapists (with further training) and arts workers. The discipline asks what music is in different cultures, how it works as sound and structure, and what it does to people and communities.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Lengths and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a university bachelor’s degree in music commonly takes four years and may be awarded as BA Music or BMus; some institutions use other titles. Polytechnic programmes usually follow the ND and HND pattern, each commonly two years, with industrial attachment between them. The National Universities Commission (NUC) guides university programmes and the National Board for Technical Education (NBTE) guides polytechnic programmes. In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s degree is commonly three years, though some programmes are four. In the United States, a bachelor’s degree is commonly four years. Master’s awards include MA, MMus and MSc, and doctoral awards include PhD and DMA; titles and lengths vary. Always check your own handbook and current accreditation, because structures and regulations change.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics start with music as a discipline and the nature of sound, acoustics and hearing. You then learn rhythm, pulse and metre; pitch, notation and the staff; intervals, scales and keys; and chords with the basics of harmony. Ear training and sight singing run alongside these, and keyboard skills support them. An overview of music in Africa introduces regional traditions early, so that African music is not treated as an appendix.

Core work usually adds history in three blocks: ancient times to the Renaissance; Baroque and Classical eras; Romanticism to the twentieth century. Theory continues with tonal harmony and counterpoint, musical form and analysis, and orchestration and instrumentation. Creative and practical courses cover composition and songwriting, conducting and rehearsal technique, and performance practice with applied study. Broader core areas include African music in depth, world music and ethnomusicology, music technology and recording, music psychology and psychoacoustics, the music business and music law, music education, and musician health, ethics and professional practice. Research methods lead to a project.

Master’s level is more specialised: advanced analysis (including Schenkerian analysis and set theory), advanced composition and arranging, ethnomusicology fieldwork methods, and a musicology seminar on sources, editing and a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study music by doing it. Practise little and often, slowly enough to avoid errors, and use a metronome for rhythm. Sing what you read and play what you hear; aural skills grow through daily short sessions, not last-minute cramming. Listen with the score when you can, and listen again without it.

For theory, work exercises by hand and check each step. Learn one short example for each concept: a cadence, a scale, a form. In history, connect a work to its date, place, genre, composer and one musical feature you can hear. Keep a listening log. For African and world music, learn the terms people use themselves and avoid forcing Western categories on them. In research, keep full references and check editions and sources. Protect your hearing and your body: use ear protection, take breaks, and warm up.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
A common mistake is treating notation as music itself. Notation is a guide; the sound, style and context matter. Another is neglecting aural skills while memorising theory, so that chords and intervals are only symbols. Students also practise fast and repeat mistakes, then find the errors hard to remove.

In history, lists of names and dates without listening produce shallow answers. In analysis, students label chords without explaining function or phrase. They may assume Western tonal theory applies everywhere, or treat African music as one tradition. In law and business, they quote another country’s rules as if universal. In research, small samples and unclear questions weaken conclusions. In performance, ignoring period style or the composer’s markings is a fault; so is ignoring hearing care and practice injury.

keyPoints: Music is both an art and an academic discipline, studied through sound, notation, history, theory and practice.
Music degrees differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook for length, award and regulations.
Aural skills, keyboard skills and listening should be practised regularly from the start.
Theory and analysis are tools for understanding music, not substitutes for hearing it.
African and world musics must be studied on their own terms, not forced into Western categories.
In law, business and health, rules and advice differ by country and change, so use current official sources.

en.title: What Is Music? The Study of Music as a Discipline
en.short: Defines music and outlines theory, history, performance, composition, ethnomusicology and music technology.

sections.heading: Defining music
sections.text:
Music is sound organised in time by people for listening, ceremony, dance, worship or play. The word covers many practices, and cultures draw the line between music and noise differently. A useful first-year definition is therefore broad: music is humanly organised sound that a community treats as music. This keeps the focus on intention and context, not only on pleasant sound.

Because the category is social, scholars avoid one universal test. A drum pattern, a chant or a recorded beat can all count. What matters is how makers and listeners use it.

sections.heading: Main branches
sections.text:
Music theory studies how music is built and described, including the materials of pitch, rhythm and harmony. Music history studies works, composers and practices in their times and places. Performance is the skilled act of playing or singing for listeners, and it includes interpretation. Composition is creating new music, from a song to a large work. Ethnomusicology studies music as part of culture, often through fieldwork, which means observing and interviewing people where they make music. Music technology covers the tools used to record, edit, notate and produce sound.

These branches overlap. A historian may use theory to analyse a score, and a performer may use history to shape interpretation.

sections.heading: Combining skills
sections.text:
Academic musicians combine listening, playing, writing and research. Listening is close and repeated attention to sound. Playing builds practical control. Writing means clear notes, essays and programme notes. Research means finding reliable sources and checking claims.

Consider Amina, a first-year student in Nairobi preparing a choral piece for a recital. She listens to two recordings, practises her part slowly, reads about the composer, and writes short programme notes. She uses theory to name the key and history to explain the style. Her teacher checks her sources. The four activities support one another.

keyPoints: Music is humanly organised sound that a community treats as music; definitions vary by culture.
The main branches are theory, history, performance, composition, ethnomusicology and music technology.
Theory describes how music is built; history studies music in context.
Ethnomusicology studies music as culture, often through fieldwork.
Academic musicians combine listening, playing, writing and research.
Skills reinforce one another: listening informs playing, and research informs writing.

en.title: Sound, Acoustics and the Ear
en.short: The physics of sound waves, pitch, loudness, timbre, harmonics, resonance, decibels and the ear.

sections.heading: Waves and pitch
sections.text: Sound is a pressure wave in a medium such as air. A vibrating source creates compressions and rarefactions. Frequency is cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). Amplitude is the size of the pressure change. Wavelength is the distance between matching points on successive cycles. In air at about 20 °C, sound travels at roughly 343 m/s, and v = f × λ. For 440 Hz, λ = 343 ÷ 440 = 0.78 m, about 78 cm. Pitch is perceived highness or lowness; doubling frequency raises it by an octave. Loudness is perceived strength and depends on amplitude and frequency, not amplitude alone.

sections.heading: Timbre and resonance
sections.text: Timbre, or tone colour, is what makes a trumpet and a violin differ on the same note. It comes mainly from the harmonic spectrum and the sound’s attack and decay. A harmonic is a component at a whole-number multiple of the fundamental frequency. A 220 Hz fundamental has harmonics at 440 Hz, 660 Hz and so on, and their relative strengths shape timbre. Resonance occurs when a system is driven near a natural frequency and vibrates strongly. A blown bottle, a violin body and a room can resonate, reinforcing some frequencies and weakening others.

sections.heading: The ear and decibels
sections.text: The outer ear funnels sound to the eardrum. The middle ear’s three small bones pass the vibration to the cochlea, a fluid-filled spiral in the inner ear. There the basilar membrane responds to different frequencies, and hair cells convert motion into nerve signals. Human hearing usually spans about 20 Hz to 20 kHz when young; the upper limit falls with age. Sound level is often given in decibels (dB). For sound pressure level, dB = 20 log10(p ÷ p0), where p0 is 20 micropascals in air. A pressure 10 times p0 is 20 dB; 100 times is 40 dB. The scale is logarithmic.

keyPoints: Sound is a pressure wave; frequency is cycles per second in hertz, amplitude is pressure-change size, and wavelength is distance between successive matching points.
Speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by v = f × λ; at about 20 °C in air, v is about 343 m/s.
Pitch relates mainly to frequency, loudness to amplitude and frequency, and timbre to harmonic spectrum and envelope.
Harmonics are whole-number multiples of the fundamental; resonance is strong vibration near a natural frequency.
The ear funnels sound to the eardrum, passes it through middle-ear bones to the cochlea, where hair cells produce nerve signals.
Sound pressure level in dB is 20 log10(p ÷ p0), with p0 = 20 micropascals in air; human hearing spans about 20 Hz to 20 kHz when young.

en.title: Rhythm, Pulse and Metre
en.short: Pulse, beat, tempo, note and rest values, simple and compound metre, ties and syncopation.

sections.heading: Pulse, beat and tempo
sections.text: Pulse is a steady underlying tick, felt or counted. A beat is the pulse chosen as the main counting unit. Tempo is the speed of the beat, usually given in beats per minute (BPM). If a metronome marks 60 BPM, there is one beat each second; at 120 BPM there are two. Tempo words such as adagio and allegro are approximate, and their meanings have changed over history, so a metronome mark is more exact.

sections.heading: Note and rest values
sections.text: Note values show relative duration. A semibreve (whole note) is usually the longest basic value; a minim is half, a crotchet one quarter, a quaver one eighth and a semiquaver one sixteenth. Rests have matching values: a crotchet rest lasts as long as a crotchet. A dot adds half the value: a dotted crotchet = 1 + 1/2 = 1.5 crotchets. A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one sound lasting their combined value.

sections.heading: Metre and time signatures
sections.text: Metre groups beats into bars. A time signature has two numbers: the top gives the number of units per bar, and the bottom gives the note value of each unit. In 4/4 there are four crotchet units per bar. Simple metre divides each beat into two; 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 are simple. Compound metre divides each beat into three; 6/8 has two dotted-crotchet beats per bar, not six quaver beats. The upper number in compound time is a multiple of three greater than three: 6, 9 or 12.

sections.heading: Subdivision and syncopation
sections.text: Subdivision is dividing a beat into smaller parts, such as quavers or semiquavers. Syncopation places stress on a weak beat or between beats, often by accent or tie. Example: in 4/4, a crotchet tied to the first quaver of beat two shifts the attack off the beat. Counting aloud, 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and, helps. Write rhythm with clear spacing, stems and beams, and check that each bar adds to the time signature.

keyPoints: Pulse is the steady tick; beat is the pulse used for counting; tempo is its speed in BPM.
Note values are relative: minim = 2 crotchets, quaver = 1/2 crotchet, semiquaver = 1/4 crotchet.
A dot adds half the note’s value: dotted crotchet = 1 + 1/2 = 1.5 crotchets.
A tie joins same-pitch notes into one duration equal to their sum.
In simple metre each beat divides into two; in compound metre each beat divides into three, as in 6/8 with two dotted-crotchet beats per bar.
Syncopation stresses a weak beat or offbeat, and subdivision divides a beat into smaller equal parts.

en.title: Pitch, Notation and the Staff
en.short: Covers reading and writing pitch: grand staff, clefs, ledger lines, accidentals, enharmonic notes and octaves.

sections.heading: Staff and clefs
sections.text:
Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Standard notation writes pitch on a staff of five lines and four spaces. A clef fixes which line or space names which pitch. The treble clef, or G clef, curls around the second line up, G4. Its lines are E4 G4 B4 D5 F5; its spaces are F4 A4 C5 E5. The bass clef, or F clef, has two dots around the fourth line up, F3. Its lines are G2 B2 D3 F3 A3; its spaces are A2 C3 E3 G3.

The grand staff joins treble and bass staves with a brace. Middle C, written C4, sits on a ledger line between them: one below the treble staff and one above the bass staff. Ledger lines are short extra lines for pitches outside a staff’s range.

sections.heading: Naming and writing
sections.text: Note names repeat in octaves using the letters C D E F G A B. Scientific pitch notation adds a number: C4 is middle C, and C4 up to B4 is the fourth octave. To read a melody, identify the clef, then count lines and spaces from a known line. To write one, place each note head on the correct line or space and add ledger lines when needed. Example: in treble clef, the bottom space is F4; one ledger line below the staff is C4.

sections.heading: Accidentals and enharmonics
sections.text:
A sharp (♯) raises a note by one semitone, a flat (♭) lowers it by one semitone, and a natural (♮) cancels a previous sharp or flat. On the piano, semitones are adjacent keys. Black keys come in groups of two and three; C is the white key just left of a group of two black keys.

Enharmonic notes are different names for the same piano key. For example, C sharp (C♯) and D flat (D♭) are enharmonic; so are F sharp and G flat. They sound the same in equal temperament, though written differently to suit the context.

keyPoints: A staff has five lines and four spaces; a clef fixes the pitch names on it.
Treble clef lines are E4 G4 B4 D5 F5; bass clef lines are G2 B2 D3 F3 A3.
Middle C is C4 and lies on a ledger line between treble and bass staves on the grand staff.
Ledger lines extend the staff for notes above or below its range.
A sharp raises by a semitone, a flat lowers by a semitone, and a natural cancels either.
Enharmonic notes such as C sharp and D flat name the same piano key in equal temperament.

en.title: Intervals, Scales and Keys
en.short: Intervals, major and minor scales, chromatic and whole-tone scales, key signatures and the circle of fifths.

sections.heading: Intervals
sections.text: An interval is the distance between two pitches. Its number counts letter names inclusively: C to E is a third. Its quality comes from semitones: a major third has 4 semitones, a minor third 3. Perfect intervals are unison, fourth, fifth and octave. Augmented is one semitone wider than major or perfect; diminished is one semitone narrower than perfect or minor. Example: C to A is 9 semitones, a major sixth; C to A-flat is 8, a minor sixth.

sections.heading: Scales
sections.text: A major scale follows T T S T T T S (tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone). A natural minor scale uses T S T T S T T. Harmonic minor raises the seventh; melodic minor raises the sixth and seventh ascending and usually returns to natural minor descending. These are common-practice conventions, not universal rules. A chromatic scale moves by semitones; a whole-tone scale moves by whole tones and has six notes per octave. Example: A major is A B C# D E F# G# A, with tonic triad A C# E.

sections.heading: Keys and identification
sections.text: A key signature is the sharps or flats after the clef. Sharps appear in the order F C G D A E B; flats in the order B E A D G C F. The circle of fifths arranges keys by perfect fifths: C, G, D, A, E, B, F# (or Gb), adding a sharp or removing a flat at each step. Each major key has a relative minor a minor third below, with the same signature: C major and A minor. The tonic triad uses degrees 1, 3 and 5. To identify a key, read the signature, then check the final note, recurring accidentals and tonic triad. For D major, the signature is F# and C#; the scale is D E F# G A B C# D; the tonic triad is D F# A, major.

keyPoints: An interval’s number counts letter names inclusively, and its quality comes from the semitone distance.
Major scale pattern: T T S T T T S; natural minor: T S T T S T T.
Harmonic minor raises the seventh; melodic minor raises the sixth and seventh ascending.
Sharps follow F C G D A E B; flats follow B E A D G C F.
The circle of fifths orders keys by perfect fifths, and each major key has a relative minor with the same signature.
A tonic triad is built on degrees 1, 3 and 5 of the scale.

en.title: Chords and the Basics of Harmony
en.short: Triads, inversions, seventh chords, symbols, diatonic chords, cadences and simple progressions.

sections.heading: Building triads
sections.text: A triad is a chord of three notes built in thirds from a scale: root, third and fifth. A major triad has four semitones from root to third and three from third to fifth. A minor triad reverses these: three then four. Diminished and augmented triads alter the fifth. For example, D major is D-F#-A: D to F# is four semitones, F# to A is three. Its first inversion is F#-A-D, with the third in the bass; second inversion is A-D-F#, with the fifth in the bass. Chord symbols may show this as D/F# or D/A.

sections.heading: Seventh chords and symbols
sections.text: A seventh chord adds a fourth note, a seventh above the root. The dominant seventh, written G7, is a major triad plus a minor seventh: G-B-D-F. Chord symbols are shorthand: C means C major, Cm C minor, Cdim C diminished, C7 C dominant seventh, Cmaj7 C major seventh. Inversions can be shown by a slash and bass note, such as C/E, or by figured bass numbers.

sections.heading: Diatonic chords
sections.text: Diatonic chords use only notes of the key. In C major the triads are I C, ii Dm, iii Em, IV F, V G, vi Am and vii° Bdim. Uppercase numerals mean major, lowercase minor, ° diminished, + augmented. Minor keys vary because natural, harmonic and melodic minor differ. In A harmonic minor, for example, the common chords are i Am, ii° Bdim, III+ C augmented, iv Dm, V E, VI F and vii° G#dim. The raised leading tone makes V major.

sections.heading: Cadences and progressions
sections.text: A cadence is a closing formula that creates or denies resolution. An authentic cadence moves V to I, a plagal cadence IV to I, a half cadence pauses on V, and a deceptive cadence moves V to vi. Progressions group chords by function: tonic (I), subdominant (IV) and dominant (V). A common progression is I-IV-V-I, in C: C-F-G-C. In minor, i-iv-V-i is common. Smooth voice leading, moving each part by small steps, helps chords connect.

keyPoints: A triad stacks root, third and fifth; a major triad has 4 semitones from root to third and 3 from third to fifth, while a minor triad reverses these.
Inversions are named by the bass note: root position, first inversion with the third in the bass, and second inversion with the fifth in the bass.
A dominant seventh chord is a major triad plus a minor seventh, for example G7 = G-B-D-F.
Diatonic triads in a major key are I ii iii IV V vi vii°, with uppercase for major and lowercase for minor.
Common cadences are authentic V-I, plagal IV-I, half ending on V, and deceptive V-vi.
A simple tonal progression is I-IV-V-I, for example C-F-G-C in C major.

en.title: Ear Training and Sight Singing
en.short: Solfège and tonic sol-fa, sight singing, dictation, interval and chord recognition, error detection.

sections.heading: Why the ear comes first
sections.text:
Music is sound, so every other subject in the course rests on hearing. A student who can name what she hears follows harmony, form and rehearsal work with far more confidence. Aural work also exposes the gap between knowing a rule on paper and hearing it in sound.

Most music schools run this as a regular practical class with tests, but the timing, weighting and pass mark vary between institutions, so check your own syllabus rather than trusting a figure from another school.

sections.heading: Solfège and tonic sol-fa
sections.text:
Solfège names the notes of a scale with syllables: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti. In fixed do, do is always C. In movable do, do is the keynote of whatever key you are singing, so one set of syllables fits every key.

Tonic sol-fa is the movable system taught by John Curwen in nineteenth-century England, spelt doh, ray, me, fah, soh, lah, te. It remains common in school and church choirs in Nigeria and elsewhere in Africa. Both systems train the same skill: hearing a scale degree and singing it true.

sections.heading: Singing at sight
sections.text:
Sight singing means performing an unseen melody from notation. Keep the pulse going even when a note is wrong, because stopping to correct breaks the rhythm, and rhythm is usually the bigger error. Look a bar ahead, and use syllables to fix the pitch relationships rather than guessing.

Short daily practice beats one long weekly session. Sing the scale and its common leaps each day and reading speed improves steadily.

sections.heading: Dictation and recognition
sections.text:
Dictation reverses sight singing: you hear music and write it down. Rhythmic dictation asks for note values and metre; melodic dictation adds pitch. Interval recognition names the distance between two notes, and chord recognition names a chord’s quality.

Useful anchors: C up to G is a perfect fifth, seven semitones, and C to the next C is an octave, twelve semitones. Error detection means spotting a wrong note or rhythm in a performance or a printed part. A singer who hears the alto sing fah where the score has me has used exactly that skill.

keyPoints: Aural skills turn written theory into heard sound and support every other music subject.
Fixed do keeps do as C; movable do makes do the keynote of the current key.
Tonic sol-fa is Curwen’s movable system, spelt doh ray me fah soh lah te.
In sight singing, keep the pulse going even after a wrong note.
Rhythmic dictation records note values and metre; melodic dictation adds pitch.
A perfect fifth is seven semitones and an octave is twelve.

en.title: Keyboard Skills and Musicianship
en.short: Keyboard technique, scales, arpeggios, piano reading, harmonisation, transposition and simple improvisation.

sections.heading: Technique first
sections.text: Good keyboard technique starts with posture: sit tall, feet supported, shoulders relaxed, and keep the wrist level and free. A rounded hand shape lets the fingers work while the arm supplies weight. Practise slowly with a steady pulse, hands separately then together, and choose fingering that repeats comfortably. Technique serves music: even tone and control let you play phrases, not just notes.

sections.heading: Scales and arpeggios
sections.text: Scales train the hand to move across the keyboard. In a scale, the thumb passes under or a finger crosses over so the line continues smoothly. Play major and minor scales slowly, listening for even tone and correct fingering. Arpeggios are broken chords played one note at a time; they teach hand shifts and chord shapes. Use a metronome, a steady-beat device, to check timing, then increase speed only when clean.

sections.heading: Reading and harmonising
sections.text: Reading at the piano joins the grand staff, the two staves joined, with treble and bass clefs, to the layout of the keys. Read by patterns: intervals, chords and bass lines, not one note at a time. Harmonisation means choosing chords to support a melody. Example: a melody ending on C in C major can use F, then G, then C chords, a common closing pattern. Check each melody note against its chord.

sections.heading: Transposing and improvising
sections.text: Transposition moves music to a new key while keeping the same intervals. To transpose a C major melody up a whole step, two semitones, to D major, C becomes D, E becomes F# and G becomes A. Simple improvisation means making music in the moment within chosen patterns. Begin with a repeated bass pattern and a five-note scale. Keyboard work supports theory by making intervals and chords visible, composition by testing ideas, and rehearsal by giving pitches and accompanying.

keyPoints: Relaxed posture, a rounded hand and slow steady practice build reliable keyboard technique.
Scales and arpeggios train even tone, fingering and smooth hand shifts.
Read piano music by patterns such as intervals, chords and bass lines.
Harmonisation fits chords to a melody and a bass line, checking each melody note.
Transposition keeps the same intervals; up a whole step, C becomes D and E becomes F#.
Simple improvisation uses chosen patterns, and keyboard work supports theory, composition and rehearsal.

en.title: Music in Africa: An Overview
en.short: Drums, ensembles, call and response, polyrhythm, talking drums, griots and music in social life.

sections.heading: One continent, many musics
sections.text: Africa is not one style. North African traditions, such as the Arab-Andalusian music of Morocco and Algeria, belong to a Mediterranean and Islamic world of modes. South of the Sahara, music differs by region and language: Mande music in Mali and Guinea, Ewe music in Ghana and Yoruba music in Nigeria, Ethiopian song, Central African vocal polyphony, southern African mbira. Some features recur, but they are tendencies, not rules. Not all African music uses drums.

sections.heading: Drums and ensembles
sections.text:
An ensemble is a group playing together. A typical drum ensemble has a lead or master drummer, supporting drums, and a bell or rattle that repeats a pattern called the timeline. The master cues changes.

Polyrhythm means several rhythms sounding at once. Cross-rhythm is a pattern whose accents fall against the main beat, so the listener feels two pulses together. Example: a bell striking two even strokes while a drum strikes three in the same span gives a 3:2 cross-rhythm.

sections.heading: Call, response, speech
sections.text:
Call and response is a dialogue: a soloist sings or plays a phrase and a chorus answers, often overlapping. It shapes much work music, worship and praise.

Talking drums exploit tone. In tone languages such as Yoruba, pitch carries meaning, so a drummer can vary the drum’s tension and reproduce spoken phrases. The Yoruba dundun family is hourglass-shaped; squeezing the cords raises the pitch. The Akan atumpan pair in Ghana is also used to send messages.

sections.heading: Griots and social life
sections.text:
Griots, called jeliw in Mande, are hereditary professional musicians and historians in Mali, Guinea, Senegal and Gambia. They sing praise, recite genealogy and play instruments such as the kora, a 21-string harp-lute, and the balafon, a wooden xylophone.

Music marks work, ritual and social life: work songs set the pace for farming, fishing or pounding; drums and song mark naming ceremonies, weddings and funerals; religious music ranges from Islamic chant to Christian choral singing. Custom often decides who may play which instrument.

keyPoints: Africa is not one musical style; regions and languages differ, and North African traditions differ from sub-Saharan ones.
A drum ensemble usually has a master drummer, supporting drums and a bell or rattle playing a repeated timeline.
Polyrhythm is several rhythms at once; cross-rhythm sets accents against the main beat, as in a 3:2 pattern.
Call and response sets a soloist’s phrase against an answering chorus.
Talking drums work because in tone languages pitch carries meaning, so drum pitch can reproduce speech.
Griots, or jeliw, are hereditary Mande professionals who praise, recite history and play kora and balafon.

en.title: Music History I: Ancient Times to the Renaissance
en.short: Ancient Greek music, plainchant, Notre Dame polyphony, Ars Nova, Renaissance mass and motet, Josquin and Palestrina.

sections.heading: Ancient music and chant
sections.text:
Ancient Greek writings on music theory survive, but very little Greek music does. Greek thinkers linked scales or modes to ethos, the character a piece could encourage.

In the medieval West, the church shaped music most. Plainchant is monophonic Latin liturgical song, sung without harmony; Gregorian chant is one family of it. Neumes, early signs above words, helped singers remember melodies. Church modes, not modern major and minor, organised chant.

sections.heading: Polyphony and Ars Nova
sections.text:
From the twelfth century, Paris Cathedral became a centre of polyphony, music in more than one part. Organum added one or more voices to plainchant. Leoninus and Perotinus are linked to the Magnus Liber Organi, a collection of organum; rhythmic modes gave the added voices repeating patterns.

In fourteenth-century France, the Ars Nova, named after a treatise by Philippe de Vitry, refined mensural notation, whose note shapes show duration. Guillaume de Machaut wrote isorhythmic motets, in which the tenor repeats a melody and a rhythm in shifting combinations, and an early complete polyphonic Mass. Such music served the church and, in chansons, the court.

sections.heading: Renaissance mass and motet
sections.text:
In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, sacred polyphony centred on the mass, a setting of the Mass Ordinary, the fixed texts of the Eucharist service, and the motet, a Latin sacred work on a biblical or liturgical text. Composers used cantus firmus, a borrowed melody often taken from chant, and imitation, in which voices share a melodic idea in turn.

Josquin des Prez, a Franco-Flemish composer, worked in chapels and courts. His Missa Pange lingua paraphrases a chant hymn across the mass. Palestrina, working in Rome, wrote clear, balanced church music; his Missa Papae Marcelli is often studied for its careful declamation. The story that Palestrina saved polyphony at the Council of Trent, the Catholic reform council, is unreliable.

sections.heading: Church and court
sections.text:
Plainchant and organum belonged to the church. Ars Nova motets and chansons served both church and court. Renaissance masses and motets were mainly for church; chansons and instrumental music for courts.

Patrons, bishops, princes and city councils often paid composers. This support shaped what was written and performed.

keyPoints: Ancient Greek music theory survives in writings, but little Greek music itself survives.
Plainchant is monophonic Latin church song; Gregorian chant is one family of it.
Notre Dame organum by Leoninus and Perotinus added voices to chant; rhythmic modes shaped the added parts.
Ars Nova notation, linked to Philippe de Vitry, showed note duration and supported Machaut’s isorhythmic motets and Mass.
Renaissance masses and motets used cantus firmus and imitation; Josquin and Palestrina are central composers.
Church and court patrons shaped the music, and the tale that Palestrina saved polyphony at Trent is unreliable.

en.title: Music History II: Baroque and Classical Eras
en.short: Covers opera, basso continuo, Baroque genres, Bach and Handel, Classical style, sonata form, symphony and concert life.

sections.heading: Opera and continuo
sections.text: Opera emerged in Italy around 1600, when composers set drama to continuous music for court audiences. Public opera theatres opened in Venice from 1637. Monteverdi’s L’Orfeo (1607) is an early masterpiece. Basso continuo is the supporting bass line played by a bass instrument and a chordal instrument such as harpsichord or lute; figures written under the bass line tell the player which chords to play. It gave singers flexible accompaniment and became the harmonic foundation of Baroque music.

sections.heading: Baroque genres and masters
sections.text: Baroque instrumental music developed the concerto and the sonata. A concerto contrasts a soloist or small group with the orchestra, often using ritornello form, where the orchestra returns with a refrain. A sonata was a chamber work; the trio sonata uses two upper parts and continuo. J. S. Bach (1685-1750) wrote sacred cantatas, Passions, fugues and concertos. Handel (1685-1759), German-born and active in London, wrote Italian operas and English oratorios, including Messiah.

sections.heading: Classical style
sections.text: The Classical style, roughly 1750 to 1800, favours clear melody, balanced phrases and flexible harmony. Haydn and Mozart shaped the symphony and string quartet. A symphony is a large orchestral work, usually in four movements. A string quartet is for two violins, viola and cello, also usually four movements. Early Beethoven extended these forms, with stronger contrasts and longer structures.

sections.heading: Sonata form and concert life
sections.text: Sonata form is a Classical structure with an exposition (themes presented), a development (themes changed and explored) and a recapitulation (themes return, usually in the home key). Public concert life grew in eighteenth-century European cities: ticketed concerts, subscription series and concert societies gave composers audiences beyond courts and churches. This encouraged independent careers and music written for public halls. The example of Haydn’s London visits shows a composer writing symphonies for a paying concert audience.

keyPoints: Opera emerged in Italy around 1600 and combined drama with continuous music.
Basso continuo is a bass line with chordal accompaniment, often guided by figures.
Baroque concertos contrast solo and orchestra, often in ritornello form, while trio sonatas use two upper parts and continuo.
Bach worked mainly in German church and court posts; Handel built a career in London with opera and oratorio.
Classical style favours clear melody and balanced phrases, and Haydn and Mozart shaped the symphony and string quartet.
Sonata form presents, develops and recapitulates themes, and public concerts gave composers new audiences and independence.

en.title: Music History III: Romanticism to the Twentieth Century
en.short: Romantic harmony, nationalism, song and opera, then modernism, Stravinsky, Bartók and minimalism.

sections.heading: Romantic expansion
sections.text: Romantic music, roughly the nineteenth century, reacted against Classical balance by favouring strong emotion, individual expression and colour. Harmony became more chromatic: composers used notes outside the key, added-note chords and dissonances that resolved later or not at all. Forms grew looser and more personal, including the character piece, the song cycle and the symphonic poem, a one-movement orchestral work with a story or scene.

sections.heading: Song, opera, nation
sections.text: The art song, or Lied, sets a poem for voice and piano. In Schubert’s Erlkönig one singer portrays narrator, father, son and Erlking, while the piano’s rapid figures suggest galloping; the song is through-composed, with new music for each stanza. Grand opera, by contrast, is large-scale French opera, typically in several acts, with chorus, ballet and spectacle. Nationalism used folk melodies, rhythms and national history; examples include Sibelius’s Finlandia and Dvořák’s Slavonic Dances.

sections.heading: Modernist break
sections.text: Modernism around 1900 rejected Romantic warmth and tonal certainty. Impressionism, associated with Debussy, stressed timbre, whole-tone and pentatonic scales, and blurred harmony; Debussy disliked the label. Atonality, as in early Schoenberg, avoids a key centre. Serialism goes further: the twelve pitch classes are ordered in a row, and the row and its forms govern melody and harmony. Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring shocked listeners with shifting metre and dissonant chords; Bartók combined folk modes with complex rhythm.

sections.heading: After 1945
sections.text: After 1945, total serialism extended rows to rhythm and dynamics, while aleatory music left choices to performers. Minimalism reacted against that complexity with repeated short patterns, steady pulse and slow change, as in Reich and Glass. Each current answered the one before: Romanticism against Classical restraint, modernism against Romantic expression, minimalism against serialist density.

keyPoints: Romantic harmony expanded tonality through chromaticism and delayed or avoided resolution.
Nationalism used folk material and national subjects within Romantic and later styles.
The art song sets a poem for voice and piano; grand opera is large-scale spectacle.
Impressionism favoured timbre and ambiguous scales; atonality abandoned a key centre.
Serialism orders all twelve pitch classes; Stravinsky and Bartók used rhythm and folk sources.
Minimalism reacted against post-war complexity with repetition and steady pulse.

en.title: Tonal Harmony and Counterpoint
en.short: Four-part writing, voice leading, chromatic harmony, modulation and species counterpoint.

sections.heading: Four-part writing
sections.text: Four-part writing sets soprano, alto, tenor and bass (SATB). Voice leading is how each part moves between chords. Keep common tones, prefer stepwise motion, and use contrary motion at cadences. Avoid parallel perfect fifths and octaves between any two voices. Double stable tones, usually the root, and resolve tendency tones: the leading tone rises to the tonic, and a chord seventh falls by step. In C major, G7 (G B D F) goes to C (C E G C); B rises to C and F falls to E.

sections.heading: Chromatic harmony
sections.text: Non-chord tones are notes outside the current chord: passing tones fill a step, suspensions hold then resolve down, and neighbour tones return. Modulation changes key, confirmed by a cadence in the new key. A secondary dominant is the V of another key, written V/V; in C major, D major (D F-sharp A) leads to G. The Neapolitan is a major triad on the lowered second degree, usually in first inversion, especially in minor. An augmented sixth chord contains an augmented sixth, for example A-flat and F-sharp in C, resolving outward to G.

sections.heading: Species counterpoint
sections.text: Species counterpoint teaches counterpoint in stages. First species is note against note; second species has two notes against one; third has four; fourth uses syncopation and suspensions; fifth is florid or free. Use consonant intervals on strong beats, approach perfect consonances by contrary motion, and keep a clear melodic climax. Free counterpoint combines these controls with imitation and varied rhythm.

sections.heading: Analysis and practice
sections.text: To analyse, label chords by Roman numeral and inversion, mark non-chord tones, and trace the key plan. To write, set the bass and soprano first, then fill inner voices. Sing each line to test it. Revise any parallel fifths or octaves, unresolved sevenths or leading tones, and awkward leaps. The rules describe tonal style, not moral laws; composers break them for effect, but the reasons remain audible.

keyPoints: Four-part writing uses SATB and avoids parallel perfect fifths and octaves.
Tendency tones resolve: the leading tone rises to the tonic and a chord seventh falls by step.
Non-chord tones decorate chords, and modulation is confirmed by a cadence in the new key.
A secondary dominant is the V of another key; the Neapolitan is a lowered-second major triad; an augmented sixth resolves outward.
Species counterpoint moves from note against note to florid free counterpoint.
Analysis labels Roman numerals and inversions and checks the voice leading.

en.title: Musical Form and Analysis
en.short: Phrase and period, binary and ternary, rondo, variation and sonata form, with score labels and listening.

sections.heading: Phrase and period
sections.text: A phrase is a short musical unit that ends with a cadence, a closing gesture. A period pairs an opening antecedent phrase with an answering consequent phrase. In a made-up eight-bar tune, two four-bar phrases, the first ending on a half cadence (an unfinished close) and the second on an authentic cadence (a finished close on the tonic, the home note), make a period. The second phrase often repeats or varies the first. Analysts label phrases a, a′ and b, and mark cadences by bar number.

sections.heading: Binary, ternary, rondo
sections.text: Form gives shape by organising repetition and contrast. Binary form has two parts, A and B, often each repeated. B may bring back A material near its end, which is rounded binary. Ternary form is A B A, with a full return of the opening. Rondo is ABACA or a similar pattern, with a recurring refrain A and contrasting episodes B and C. To hear form, listen for repetition, contrast and return, then mark the bar numbers where each section begins. A label alone is not analysis; say what the return changes.

sections.heading: Variation and sonata form
sections.text: Variation form states a theme (a melodic idea), then repeats it with changes to melody, harmony, rhythm or tone colour while keeping it recognisable. Sonata form is a large design in three main stages. The exposition presents themes, usually a first subject and a second subject in contrasting keys. The development breaks up and recombines them. The recapitulation returns them, normally with the second subject in the tonic. A coda may close the movement. Sonata form is flexible, not a fixed mould. Label the exposition, transition, subjects, development, recapitulation and coda, then write short prose: what happens at bar 21, and why does it matter?

keyPoints: A phrase ends with a cadence; a period pairs an antecedent phrase with a consequent phrase.
Binary form is A B; ternary form is A B A; rondo uses a recurring refrain.
Variation form keeps a theme recognisable while changing its surface.
Sonata form normally moves from exposition to development to recapitulation, but it is flexible.
Good analysis combines labels with short prose explaining what happens and why.
Listen for repetition, contrast and return to hear form.

en.title: Orchestration and Instrumentation: Writing for Ensembles
en.short: Ranges, transpositions, tone colours, score layout, balance and writing for orchestral, band and African ensembles.

sections.heading: Ranges and transposition
sections.text:
Orchestration is choosing and combining instruments; instrumentation is the study of the instruments themselves. Every instrument has a comfortable and an extreme range, and these differ between players and makers, so check a reliable text or the player.

Transposing instruments are written at a pitch different from sounding pitch. A B-flat clarinet sounds a major second lower than written; a horn in F sounds a perfect fifth lower; the piccolo sounds an octave higher and the double bass an octave lower. Notate for the player, not the sound.

sections.heading: Tone colour and balance
sections.text:
Tone colour, or timbre, is the quality that distinguishes a flute from a violin on the same note. It changes with register, dynamics and articulation: a low flute is breathy, a high violin can be brilliant.

Doubling gives the same line to two instruments. It adds weight and colour, but can blur detail in a crowded register. Balance keeps melody, bass and inner parts in proportion. Put important lines where the instrument is clear, and leave space around them.

sections.heading: Score layout and reading
sections.text:
A full orchestral score normally groups woodwind, brass, percussion and strings, each family in a fixed order; band and ensemble scores vary, so read the instrument list first. Study clefs, transpositions and brackets.

African ensembles often work without a full score: parts may be taught by ear, written as cipher or lead sheets, or set in staff notation. Do not assume one practice is universal. Mark rehearsal figures, dynamics and articulations.

sections.heading: Choosing and writing
sections.text:
Writing for a small ensemble demands independence: each part must be complete and audible. A large ensemble allows mass, contrast and doublings, but too much doubling makes a thick, dull texture.

Choose instruments for the effect you want: a bright attack for a call, a sustained low sound for weight, a delicate high line for tension. A case: a university ensemble in Lagos, Nigeria might give a call-and-response melody to talking drum and trumpet, with a keyboard pad beneath. Check with players.

keyPoints: Orchestration chooses and combines instruments; instrumentation studies their ranges, transpositions and tone colours.
Transposing instruments are written at a different pitch from sounding pitch, so notate for the player.
Tone colour changes with register, dynamics and articulation; doubling adds weight but can blur detail.
A full orchestral score groups families in a fixed order; band and African ensemble notation practices vary.
Balance keeps melody, bass and inner parts in proportion, and small ensembles need independent parts.
Choose instruments for the effect you want and check the result with players.

en.title: Composition and Songwriting: From Idea to Draft
en.short: Melody, motifs, harmony, texture, form, lyrics, arranging and revision for small groups.

sections.heading: Starting from an idea
sections.text: A composition can begin with a motif, a short melodic or rhythmic idea, a chord progression, a lyric line or a mood. Decide what the piece is for: a song, a choral piece, a small ensemble work. A sketch, whether sung, played or written, fixes the idea before details grow. Keep the first draft simple. In a small case, Ada hums a four-note motif, then writes a second phrase that answers it. This call and response gives the opening shape.

sections.heading: Melody and motifs
sections.text: Melody is a line of pitches and rhythms heard as one shape. Good melodies often balance steps and leaps, and repeat enough to be remembered. Motivic development means changing a motif while keeping it recognisable: sequence it higher or lower, invert it, augment it by lengthening its rhythms, or fragment it. Harmony supports the melody. Choose chords that clarify the key and give tension and release. Texture is how parts relate: melody with accompaniment, homophony, where chords move together, or polyphony, where lines move independently. For a small group, keep each part playable and give the main idea to one voice.

sections.heading: Form and lyrics
sections.text: Form is the large plan. A common song form is verse and chorus, with a bridge. An instrumental piece may use binary (AB) or ternary (ABA) shape. Lyrics need a clear speaker, concrete images and a singable stress pattern. Match stressed syllables to strong beats. Avoid forcing a rhyme if it weakens the sense.

sections.heading: Arranging and revision
sections.text: Arranging decides who plays or sings what, in what range and dynamic. For voices, respect comfortable ranges and set words so consonants are heard. For small groups, avoid doubling every line; contrast keeps interest. Revise by asking listeners or players for specific feedback: is the opening clear, is the chorus arrival strong, which bar feels weak? Test one change at a time, keep a copy of each draft, and compare. A revision succeeds when the main idea is clearer, not busier.

keyPoints: A motif is a short idea, and motivic development changes it while keeping it recognisable.
A melody balances steps and leaps and uses enough repetition to be remembered.
Harmony clarifies the key and creates tension and release, while texture describes how parts relate.
Form is the large plan, and verse and chorus or binary and ternary shapes are common starting points.
Lyrics need a clear speaker, concrete images and a stress pattern that fits the music.
Arranging assigns parts and ranges, and revision improves a draft through specific feedback and controlled changes.

en.title: Conducting and Rehearsal Technique
en.short: Beat patterns, cueing, expressive gestures, score preparation and efficient rehearsal planning.

sections.heading: Patterns and pulse
sections.text: A beat pattern is the path the conductor’s hand takes to show the metre. The ictus is the point where the beat lands. Simple metres such as 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 use two, three or four beats. Compound metres such as 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 are usually beaten in two, three or four dotted beats, each divided into three. Keep the pattern small for fast music and larger for slow music. A preparatory beat before the first sound sets tempo, dynamics and character.

sections.heading: Cues and expression
sections.text:
A cue signals an entry. Prepare it with eye contact, a breath and a gesture that arrives on the beat before the entry. The right hand mainly keeps time; the left hand can cue, ask for softer or louder playing, and give cut-offs, which end the sound. Dynamics are shown by gesture size, height and tension: a small, low gesture suggests soft; a broad, high gesture suggests loud.

Phrasing is shown by motion: a smooth, connected gesture, called legato, asks for singing tone; a short, detached gesture, called staccato, asks for separation. Balance is controlled by listening and by showing which line should lead. A conductor can rehearse without speaking by using a look, a gesture or a silent count.

sections.heading: Score and rehearsal
sections.text: Score preparation means studying the full score before rehearsal. Mark entries, cues, repeats, tempo changes and difficult transitions. Know the form, main themes and text. Write a timed rehearsal plan: warm-up, section work, integration and run-through. In an invented case, a student choir in Nairobi rehearses a 4/4 anthem. The conductor marks the alto entry at bar 12 and the transition at bars 20 to 24. They spend ten minutes on that transition, then sing the piece once. An efficient rehearsal starts with a clear goal, rehearses hard passages while minds are fresh, isolates one problem at a time, then puts it back into context. Stop only for a clear reason, give a specific instruction, and restart a little before the problem.

keyPoints: A beat pattern shows the metre; the ictus is the point of the beat.
Compound metres are usually beaten in dotted beats, each divided into three.
A preparatory beat sets tempo, dynamics and character before the first sound.
Cues use breath, eye contact and a gesture that arrives on the beat before the entry.
Dynamics and phrasing are shown by gesture size, height and continuity.
Score preparation and a timed rehearsal plan make rehearsals efficient.

en.title: Performance Practice and Applied Study
en.short: Posture, tone, practice planning, programme building, stagecraft, auditions and informed performance.

sections.heading: Posture and tone
sections.text: Posture is the alignment of the body that lets breath and movement work freely. Set the stool, stand or strap so arms and hands are relaxed; for voice, keep the neck easy and let the ribs move. Tone production is controlled use of breath, embouchure (lip setting for wind and brass players), bow or vocal folds, and resonance. Technique means reliable habits of fingers, bow, breath or articulation. Correct tension early: a singer who raises the shoulders tires; releasing the neck and breathing lower can steady the sound.

sections.heading: Practice planning
sections.text: Plan practice by goal, not time alone. Warm up, then isolate a short difficult passage, slow it down, join it to the phrase, and rest. Use a metronome or recording to check. Keep a log: date, task, tempo, result. Example: if a passage is marked at 120 beats per minute and you can play it cleanly at 80, raise the metronome by 4 beats per minute only after three clean repeats.

sections.heading: Programme and stagecraft
sections.text: A programme is the ordered list of works in a recital. Build it with contrast and coherence: open with a work you can settle into, vary mood and period, and place the most demanding item where your energy is good. Check timing and printed order. Stagecraft covers walking on, bowing, acknowledging the accompanist and handling pauses. Rehearse the whole programme in performance order, including bows. Historically informed performance (HIP) means making style choices from evidence: treatises, scores, instruments and recordings. It does not mean one correct way; practice varied by place and decade.

sections.heading: Auditions and pressure
sections.text: An audition is a short assessed performance, often with set pieces and sight-reading (performing unseen music). Read the notice carefully; requirements differ by school and country. Prepare the opening bars especially, because nerves affect starts. For pressure, use slow breathing, a simple routine and focus on the first phrase rather than the result. If a mistake happens, continue. Record mock auditions and seek feedback. Check the current official requirements.

keyPoints: Posture should allow free breath and relaxed movement, and tension should be corrected early.
Tone production combines breath, embouchure, bow or vocal folds, and resonance; technique is reliable habit.
Plan practice by specific goals, slow isolated work, rests and a written log.
Build a recital programme with contrast, coherence, realistic timing and rehearsal in performance order.
Stagecraft and mock auditions reduce pressure; audition requirements vary by institution and country.
Historically informed performance uses evidence from treatises, scores, instruments and recordings, and allows more than one valid choice.

en.title: African Music in Depth: Regions and Traditions
en.short: Yoruba dundun and bata, Igbo ekwe and ogene, Akan fontomfrom and kete, Ethiopian church music and Zimbabwean mbira.

sections.heading: Yoruba drums
sections.text: Yoruba dundun is a family of hourglass-shaped tension drums from south-west Nigeria. The player squeezes the cords between the drumheads, raising or lowering pitch, so the drum can imitate speech tones. The lead drum carries proverbs and praise; supporting drums answer. Bata is a set of double-headed drums with a separate repertoire, linked to Sango worship and social celebrations. Both are ensemble arts: rhythm is shared, not solo. Pitch is relative, tuned by ear to the group, not to a fixed Western scale.

sections.heading: Igbo and Akan
sections.text: Among Igbo people of Nigeria, ekwe is a wooden slit drum and ogene is a metal bell. Ekwe marks the pulse and sends signals; ogene plays a repeated timeline that holds the ensemble together. They appear at meetings, ceremonies and masquerades. In Akan areas of Ghana, fontomfrom is a royal drum ensemble played for chiefs, with large drums and a lead drummer. Kete is courtly music for chiefs, using drums and bells. These ensembles mark rank and community; tuning is adjusted by makers and players.

sections.heading: Ethiopian church music
sections.text: Ethiopian Orthodox church music is mainly vocal, sung in Ge’ez and other languages, and organised into three chant modes, Ge’ez, Ezel and Araray. Saint Yared is traditionally credited with founding the chant. The kebero drum and the sistrum, a metal rattle, mark time; the mode shapes melody and mood. This music is not equal-tempered Western harmony. Its tuning and intonation follow church practice, and singers learn through long training. It carries prayer, calendar and identity.

sections.heading: Mbira and tuning
sections.text: Mbira is a Zimbabwean lamellophone: metal keys fixed to a wooden board and played with the thumbs and index fingers. Mbira dzavadzimu, the 'mbira of the ancestors', is central to Shona bira ceremonies, where it is played with hosho rattles, clapping and singing. One player plays kushaura, the leading part; another may play kutsinhira, an interlocking part. The keys are tuned by the maker, and tunings vary, so the instrument is not fixed to one standard scale. The music carries memory, spirit and community.

keyPoints: Dundun pitch is changed by squeezing tension cords; bata has its own repertoire and Sango links.
Igbo ekwe and ogene divide roles: slit drum pulse and signal, metal bell timeline.
Akan fontomfrom and kete are royal or courtly ensembles that mark rank and community.
Ethiopian Orthodox chant is modal and vocal, with kebero and sistrum, learned in church practice.
Mbira dzavadzimu is a Shona lamellophone used in bira ceremonies with hosho and interlocking parts.
These traditions often tune by ear and to each other, not to one universal scale.

en.title: World Music and Ethnomusicology
en.short: Asian, Middle Eastern, American and Oceanian musics; fieldwork, transcription, organology and insider-outsider debate.

sections.heading: What ethnomusicology studies
sections.text: Ethnomusicology is the study of music as social practice: who makes it, for whom, and what it means. The label world music is a broad teaching and marketing term, not one style. The course surveys many traditions, for example Javanese gamelan in Indonesia, raga and tala in Indian classical music, maqam in Arab music, and diverse Indigenous, European and African-derived traditions in the Americas and Oceania. These are examples, not summaries of whole continents.

sections.heading: Fieldwork and ethics
sections.text: Fieldwork means going to where music is made and learning over time. Participant observation combines watching, listening, interviewing and sometimes learning to perform. Ethical fieldwork needs informed consent, clear explanation of how recordings will be used, and reciprocity, meaning giving something back. A student, Amina, plans to record a maqam session in Cairo. She asks the performers first, explains her project, shares the recording, and lets them correct her notes before she publishes.

sections.heading: Transcription and organology
sections.text: Transcription is writing heard music into notation, graphs or tables. It is always selective: a staff score may miss timbre or microtones, while a graph may miss phrasing. Check transcriptions with performers. Organology is the study of musical instruments. The Hornbostel-Sachs system groups instruments by sound production: idiophones (the body vibrates, as in a xylophone), membranophones (a skin vibrates, as in a drum), chordophones (strings, as in a lute) and aerophones (air, as in a flute). Electrophones were added later.

sections.heading: Insider and outsider
sections.text: The insider-outsider debate asks who can study a tradition. Insiders may know meanings and language deeply; outsiders may notice patterns insiders take for granted. Ethnomusicologists use emic (insider) and etic (outsider analytical) perspectives. Neither is automatically correct. Respectful study names performers, asks how they wish to be described, seeks permission for sacred or restricted material, and treats living traditions as changing, not exotic or frozen.

keyPoints: Ethnomusicology studies music in its social and cultural context, not only its sound.
World music is a broad label, not a single genre; continents contain many distinct traditions.
Fieldwork requires consent, reciprocity and community review of recordings and notes.
Transcription is selective and should be checked with performers.
Hornbostel-Sachs classifies instruments as idiophones, membranophones, chordophones and aerophones, with electrophones added later.
Emic and etic perspectives both contribute; respectful study avoids treating traditions as exotic or frozen.

en.title: Music Technology and Recording: From Microphone to Master
en.short: Microphones, signal flow, desks, DAWs, MIDI, sampling, editing, mixing, mastering and ensemble recording.

sections.heading: Microphones and signal flow
sections.text:
A microphone turns sound into an electrical signal. Its polar pattern describes sensitivity around it: omnidirectional picks up all directions, cardioid favours the front and rejects the rear, and figure-eight favours front and back. Condenser mics often need phantom power, usually 48 V, supplied by the preamp or desk; dynamic mics generally do not. Signal flow is the path from source to recording: microphone, mic preamp, analogue-to-digital converter, digital audio workstation (DAW), then monitors or export. Set gain so peaks are below clipping, the point where the converter runs out of numbers.

A clean signal depends on gain staging, meaning setting each stage so it is neither too weak nor too hot. Noise rises if gain is too low; distortion rises if it is too high.

sections.heading: Desks, DAWs and MIDI
sections.text: A mixing desk, or console, gives each input a channel strip: gain, equalisation (EQ), auxiliary sends, pan and fader. EQ changes frequency balance; an aux send feeds a shared effect such as reverb. A DAW is software for recording, editing and mixing. MIDI carries performance instructions such as note, pitch, velocity and timing, not audio. A sampler records or imports a sound and plays it back at chosen pitches; clear any copyright in the sample before release.

sections.heading: Recording an ensemble
sections.text: To record a small ensemble, place close mics for detail and a room pair for space. Check phase: if two mics hear the same source with opposite polarity, low frequencies cancel. Give players a headphone mix, label tracks, and keep one clean take. For example, one minute of uncompressed stereo 44.1 kHz, 16-bit audio needs 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 60 = 84,672,000 bits, about 10.6 MB.

sections.heading: Editing, mixing, mastering
sections.text: Editing trims takes, sets fades and crossfades, and joins the best parts. Mixing balances levels, pan, EQ, dynamics and reverb. Mastering is the final stage: controlled loudness, tonal consistency and correct export format. Export at the session’s sample rate and bit depth unless delivery requires otherwise; 24-bit is common for mixing, 16-bit for CD. Listen on several systems.

keyPoints: Polar pattern describes a microphone’s directional sensitivity: omni, cardioid or figure-eight.
Signal flow runs source, microphone, preamp, converter, DAW, then monitor or export.
A mixing desk channel strip usually has gain, EQ, aux sends, pan and fader.
MIDI carries performance data, not audio; a sampler plays recorded sounds at chosen pitches.
Phase-check close and room mics, and give ensemble players a headphone mix.
Stereo file size in bits = sample rate × bit depth × channels × seconds; one minute at 44.1 kHz/16-bit stereo is about 10.6 MB.

en.title: Music Psychology and Psychoacoustics
en.short: Pitch, loudness, timbre, critical bands, masking, tuning, expectation, memory, emotion and development.

sections.heading: Pitch, loudness, timbre
sections.text:
Psychoacoustics studies how sound becomes hearing. Pitch is the perceived highness or lowness of a tone; it depends mainly on frequency but also on loudness and timbre. Loudness is perceived intensity, not simply sound level: it changes with frequency and duration. Timbre lets us tell a flute from a violin at the same pitch and loudness.

It comes from the spectrum (which partials are present and how strong) and from how the sound changes over time, including attack and decay. These perceptual quantities need not match physical measures.

sections.heading: Bands and masking
sections.text:
The auditory system behaves like overlapping filters. A critical band is a frequency region within which sounds interact strongly. Masking occurs when one sound makes another harder to hear by raising its detection threshold. Simultaneous masking uses sounds at the same time; temporal masking uses sounds just before or after.

Masking is stronger when masker and target are close in frequency. It matters in mixing, hearing tests and how melodies survive against accompaniment.

sections.heading: Tuning and temperament
sections.text:
Tuning systems choose which frequency ratios count as intervals. Just intonation uses simple ratios such as 3:2 for a perfect fifth, giving pure intervals in one key but trouble when modulating. Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve equal semitones; each semitone ratio is 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.0595. A cent is one hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone.

Worked example: 440 Hz to 880 Hz is one octave. Cents = 1200 × log2(880 ÷ 440) = 1200 × log2(2) = 1200 cents. Equal temperament also gives twelve semitones × 100 = 1200 cents.

sections.heading: Expectation and listeners
sections.text:
Listening is active. Expectation, built from schemas and prior exposure, shapes attention; fulfilled or delayed expectations can feel pleasant, tense or moving. Memory holds short patterns and compares them with learned ones, so chunking helps. Emotion involves arousal, valence, familiarity and personal association, not notes alone.

Musical development begins with enculturation: infants notice pitch and rhythm contrasts, and training refines categories. Two listeners hear one piece differently because their cultures, training, attention, mood, memories and hearing differ.

keyPoints: Pitch depends mainly on frequency, loudness on intensity and frequency, and timbre on spectrum and time envelope.
Critical bands are frequency regions of strong interaction, and masking raises the threshold for nearby sounds.
Just intonation gives pure simple ratios in one key; equal temperament divides the octave into twelve equal semitones.
A cent is 1/100 of an equal-tempered semitone; cents = 1200 × log2(f2 ÷ f1).
Expectation, memory, emotion and enculturation shape how a listener hears a piece.
Two listeners can hear one piece differently because culture, training, attention, mood, memory and hearing differ.

en.title: The Music Business and Music Law
en.short: Roles, contracts, fees, copyright in works and recordings, and collecting societies.

sections.heading: Who is involved
sections.text: A composer writes the musical work; a lyricist writes words; both may be called songwriters. A performer plays or sings it. A publisher administers a songwriter’s copyright, licenses uses and collects money, usually for a share. A record label finances recordings and markets them. A promoter organises live concerts and pays artists or their agents a fee, sometimes sharing ticket income. A collecting society licenses broadcast or public performance and distributes royalties to members.

sections.heading: Two sets of rights
sections.text: In many countries a recorded song carries two main sets of rights: copyright in the musical work and lyrics, and rights in the sound recording. The writer or publisher owns or administers the first; the label or artist may own the second. Copyright gives exclusive rights to copy, distribute, perform and make adaptations, subject to exceptions such as fair dealing or fair use. Terms and exceptions differ by country. Check your national copyright law.

sections.heading: Contracts and fees
sections.text: Contracts set out rights transferred, territory, duration, payment and termination. A label may pay an advance, a prepayment recouped from the artist’s royalties. Royalties are percentages of income, but the base matters. Example: if a contract gives 20% of net receipts and a sale earns 1,000 naira net, the artist’s share is 0.20 × 1,000 = 200 naira before recoupment. A publisher may take a share of income for administration. Live fees may be fixed or a share of ticket sales.

sections.heading: Collecting and checks
sections.text: Collecting societies may license performance, broadcast, reproduction or mechanical uses, depending on the country. They collect from users and distribute to writers, publishers or performers. Membership, mandates and distribution rules vary. Before signing, ask which rights are assigned, for how long, in which countries, and what deductions apply. Keep split sheets and registration details. Because rights and collecting practice differ by country, check your national law and regulator, and take legal advice for a real contract.

keyPoints: Composers and lyricists create the musical work; performers bring it to performance.
Publishers administer song copyrights; labels finance and market recordings; promoters run live events.
In many countries a recorded song has separate rights in the composition and in the sound recording.
Contracts should state rights transferred, territory, duration, payment, deductions and termination.
Royalties are percentages of a defined base, so check whether the base is gross or net and how advances are recouped.
Collecting societies and copyright rules differ by country; check national law and the regulator before signing.

en.title: Music Education and Teaching Methods
en.short: Kodály, Orff and Dalcroze methods, lesson planning, classroom instruments, assessment and inclusion.

sections.heading: Three named approaches
sections.text:
Three approaches are widely taught. The Kodály method, from Zoltán Kodály in Hungary, starts with singing. It uses movable-do solfège, singing notes to syllables such as do, re and mi (do is the key note, wherever the key sits), hand signs, rhythm syllables such as ta and ti-ti, and songs from the learners’ own culture.

The Orff Schulwerk, from Carl Orff in Germany, joins speech, singing, movement and percussion. Children play short repeated patterns called ostinatos, often in pentatonic scales (five notes, no semitones), and improvise. Dalcroze eurhythmics, from Émile Jaques-Dalcroze in Switzerland, teaches rhythm through bodily movement, with solfège and improvisation.

These are models, not laws. Teachers adapt them, and many combine them with local practice.

sections.heading: Planning lessons
sections.text:
A scheme of work is the term or year overview: topics, sequence, resources and assessment points. A lesson plan covers one lesson: objectives, materials, activities, timing and how you will check learning. Write objectives as things learners will do, for example "clap a four-beat ostinato in time".

A 40-minute beginner lesson might run: 5 minutes warm-up and pulse games, 10 minutes listening, 15 minutes singing and playing, 7 minutes a short composing task, 3 minutes closing review. That is 5 + 10 + 15 + 7 + 3 = 40 minutes.

sections.heading: Classroom instruments
sections.text: Common instruments are recorders, xylophones and other barred instruments, ukuleles, keyboards and hand percussion. Where available, drums, rattles and mbira (thumb piano) can anchor a lesson in local music. Choose pentatonic parts so that any note sounds acceptable, and give each learner one part in a layered piece.

sections.heading: Assessment and inclusion
sections.text:
Formative assessment is ongoing checking during teaching; summative assessment judges achievement at the end, such as a recorded performance. Assess listening, performing and composing separately, with clear criteria shared in advance.

Inclusive teaching plans for different abilities from the start: the same song with simpler and harder parts, extra time, peer partners, and seating that allows a learner with limited mobility to play. Describe what a learner can do, not a label.

keyPoints: Kodály builds on singing, solfège and local songs; Orff on speech, movement and percussion; Dalcroze on movement.
A scheme of work covers the term; a lesson plan covers one lesson with timed stages.
Write objectives as observable actions, and share assessment criteria in advance.
Pentatonic and ostinato parts let mixed-ability classes play together.
Assess listening, performing and composing separately.
Plan for different abilities from the start rather than adapting afterwards.

en.title: Musician Health, Ethics and Professional Practice
en.short: Hearing, injury prevention, practice load, performance anxiety and professional ethics for musicians.

sections.heading: Hearing and strain
sections.text: Sound damage depends on loudness and time. Rehearsing beside a drummer or in a loud pit can harm hearing. Use musician earplugs, which lower volume without muffling too much, keep monitor levels low, and take quiet breaks. Tinnitus, ringing in the ears, and muffled hearing are warning signs; if they persist, see an audiologist, a hearing specialist. Singers should warm up, stay hydrated, avoid shouting over noise, and stop if hoarseness or pain lasts. Instrumentalists should check posture and technique, and treat pain as a signal to rest and seek medical advice.

sections.heading: Practice and rest
sections.text: Practice load is total practice time and effort. Distributed practice, short sessions with breaks, usually beats one long session. Increase demanding work gradually, and separate heavy playing from heavy singing or conducting. Sleep and rest days let tissue recover. A guitarist with forearm pain should cut practice, check technique with a teacher, and see a clinician if pain continues; pushing through can turn a minor strain into a long injury. A log of hours and symptoms helps spot patterns.

sections.heading: Performance anxiety
sections.text: Performance anxiety is fear of being judged on stage. It can cause shaking, dry mouth, racing heart and narrowed attention. Prepare thoroughly, practise performing for others, use slow breathing, and focus on the music rather than mistakes. Some arousal helps; the aim is control, not zero nerves. If anxiety stops you performing or affects daily life, seek counselling or help. Teachers should teach coping and avoid shaming.

sections.heading: Ethics and fairness
sections.text: Professional ethics means treating people with respect and honesty. Teachers need informed consent, meaning agreement after information, clear fees and boundaries, and a duty of care, the responsibility not to harm. Auditions should use clear criteria and screened rounds, with identity hidden, to reduce bias. Give credit for ideas, compositions, arrangements and recordings, and agree credit before release. When working with communities, ask permission, explain how recordings will be used, share benefits, and respect local ownership. Codes vary by country; check guidance.

keyPoints: Hearing damage depends on loudness and exposure time; use earplugs, lower levels and take quiet breaks.
Warm up, hydrate and stop singing or playing when pain or hoarseness persists; seek qualified advice.
Distributed practice with breaks and gradual increases in load protects against injury better than marathon sessions.
Performance anxiety is manageable through preparation, exposure and breathing; seek help if it impairs daily life.
Ethics requires informed consent, fair audition criteria, accurate attribution and agreed credit.
Community work needs permission, clear use of recordings, shared benefits and respect for local ownership.

en.title: Research Methods and the Music Project
en.short: Library and score research, listening analysis, citation and the shape of a music essay or final project.

sections.heading: Choosing a question
sections.text:
A research question is narrow, answerable from evidence and open to argument. “Music in Ghana” is a topic; “How does the guitar part in two 1970s highlife recordings differ in rhythmic feel?” is a question. Test it: can you find the recordings, scores and written sources you need? If not, narrow it further.

Keep a research log of what you searched, where, and what you found. It makes your method visible and saves repeated work.

sections.heading: Library and score research
sections.text:
Begin with the library catalogue and music databases. RILM (Répertoire International de Littérature Musicale) indexes writings on music, and JSTOR and your library’s own databases hold journal articles. Primary sources are made at the time or by the people you study: scores, recordings, letters. Secondary sources interpret them: books and articles.

For a score, record its full identity: composer, title, editor, publisher, place and year. An urtext edition aims to give the composer’s text without editorial additions; a performing edition may add fingering, bowing or dynamics. Name the edition you used, because those additions affect what you can claim.

sections.heading: Listening as evidence
sections.text:
Listening analysis means describing what you hear in musical terms before you interpret it. Give bar numbers or timings (mm:ss) so a reader can check your claim. Listen more than once, and compare recordings of the same work, since tempo, balance and ornamentation often differ.

Case: Amina compares two recordings of one piano piece. She writes, “In recording B the left hand is louder at bar 17”, then asks what this does to the texture. She does not claim the pianist intended it.

sections.heading: Writing and citing
sections.text:
A music essay usually has an introduction stating the question and your answer, called the thesis; sections presenting evidence in a clear order; and a conclusion that weighs the evidence. Cite every borrowed idea, quoted or paraphrased, and give bar numbers for musical points.

Citation styles differ (Chicago, Harvard, MLA and others), and music departments often add rules for scores and recordings. Check your department’s guide. Be honest: report evidence that weakens your case, keep description separate from interpretation, and state plainly what you could not establish.

keyPoints: A research question must be narrow, arguable and answerable from sources you can actually obtain.
Distinguish primary sources such as scores and recordings from secondary writings about them.
Record the edition of every score you use, since urtext and performing editions differ.
Use bar numbers or timings so readers can verify your listening claims.
Cite all borrowed ideas in the style your department requires.
Report contrary evidence and state the limits of what you could establish.

en.title: Advanced Analysis: Schenker, Set Theory and Beyond
en.short: Schenkerian reduction, pitch-class sets, neo-Riemannian theory, rhythm and form analysis.

sections.heading: Schenkerian reduction
sections.text: Schenkerian analysis, after Heinrich Schenker, treats a tonal piece as a hierarchy of levels.
