The background is the Ursatz, a fundamental line (Urlinie) over a bass arpeggiation (Bassbrechung). Middleground and foreground show prolongation, the way a harmony or motive is extended. It helps with common-practice tonal music, especially clear tonic prolongation. It leaves out rhythm, timbre and context, and is interpretive: analysts may disagree. It is not designed for post-tonal or most popular music.

sections.heading: Pitch-class sets
sections.text: Pitch-class set theory, after Allen Forte, reduces pitches to twelve pitch classes, C = 0 to B = 11, ignoring octave and register. A set is put in normal order, its most compact ordering, then prime form, the best-packed version under transposition and inversion. The interval vector counts interval classes 1 to 6. Example: C major {C,E,G} = {0,4,7}; normal order [0,4,7]; prime form (0,3,7); interval vector [0,0,1,1,1,0]. It helps with atonal and post-tonal music, motives and similarity. It leaves out rhythm, texture, timbre and tonal function.

sections.heading: Neo-Riemannian theory
sections.text: Neo-Riemannian theory, named for Hugo Riemann and developed by David Lewin and Richard Cohn, analyses triads through transformations. P moves a major triad to its parallel minor, L exchanges a major triad with the minor triad a major third above (C major to E minor), and R moves to the relative minor. Each transformation moves one voice by step and keeps two common tones, producing smooth voice leading. The Tonnetz maps them as a network. The method helps with chromatic tonal and film music. It leaves out melody, rhythm, non-triadic harmony and large-scale form.

sections.heading: Rhythm and form
sections.text: Rhythm and form analysis asks how pulse, metre, hypermetre (metre above the bar), phrase and section shape a piece. In tonal music, form may be shown by cadences and key schemes. In popular music, analysts use verse, chorus, bridge, loop and groove, and 12-bar blues. They help all repertoires and correct the pitch bias of Schenker and set theory. They leave out harmony unless combined, and they need transcription and cultural context.

keyPoints: Schenkerian analysis describes tonal music as levels from foreground to the Ursatz.
Pitch-class set theory uses integer notation C = 0 to B = 11, with arithmetic modulo 12.
Prime form is the most compact version of a set under transposition and inversion; the major triad is (0,3,7).
The interval vector counts interval classes 1 to 6; (0,3,7) has [0,0,1,1,1,0].
Neo-Riemannian P, L and R transform triads by smooth voice leading.
Rhythm and form analysis covers metre, hypermetre, phrase and popular song sections, and every method leaves out some features.

en.title: Advanced Composition and Arranging
en.short: Extended techniques, graphic scores, large and mixed ensembles, film scoring, style and part preparation.

sections.heading: Extended techniques
sections.text:
Extended techniques are ways of playing an instrument beyond its standard method: flutter-tonguing on the flute, multiphonics on the clarinet, col legno (striking the string with the wood of the bow) and sul ponticello (bowing near the bridge) on strings, and the prepared piano, where objects are placed on the strings. Each has limits of range, dynamics and reliability, so ask a player before you depend on one.

Put a short performance note in the score explaining every sign you invent, and give players time to learn it in rehearsal.

sections.heading: New notation and graphic scores
sections.text:
Contemporary scores often mix the staff with proportional notation, where horizontal space stands for time rather than bars, and with graphic scores, where drawings, shapes or lines replace conventional notes. Indeterminate or aleatory passages leave choices to the performer, through loose instructions or a mobile form whose sections can be reordered.

Krzysztof Penderecki’s Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima (1960) uses dense graphic clusters. Always print a legend, a key explaining each symbol. Without it the score cannot be read.

sections.heading: Large ensembles and film
sections.text:
Large-ensemble writing is a balance of weight: doubling a line across sections thickens it but can dull detail. Mixed ensembles, such as choir with strings or electronics with wind band, raise questions of balance, amplification and who leads.

Film and media scoring adds timing. A spotting session fixes where each cue, one piece of music for the film, starts and stops, and a click track keeps players with the picture. A cue of 1 minute 30 seconds at 90 beats per minute in 4/4 needs 90 × 1.5 = 135 beats, and 135 ÷ 4 = 33.75, so about 34 bars.

sections.heading: Style and parts
sections.text:
Personal style grows from deliberate imitation and then deviation: study models closely, then change one parameter at a time until the voice is yours.

Part preparation is craft. Transpose parts for transposing instruments, add cue notes from other players, plan page turns during rests, number bars and mark rehearsal letters. Check every part against the score. Arranging or copying an existing work usually needs permission from the copyright owner.

keyPoints: Extended techniques need a player’s advice and a written performance note.
Proportional notation uses space for time; graphic scores use shapes instead of conventional notes.
Every graphic or invented symbol needs a legend the performer can read.
Aleatory notation gives the performer controlled choices, not no control.
Film cues are timed to picture with a spotting session and a click track.
Good part preparation, with transposition, cues and page turns, is part of composition.

en.title: Ethnomusicology: Fieldwork, Ethics and Research Methods
en.short: Research design, ethics, fieldwork, recording, transcription, analysis and fair write-up.

sections.heading: Design and ethics
sections.text:
Research design states the question, site, participants and methods. In ethnomusicology the question often concerns how music is made, taught, valued or used, not only how it sounds. Match methods to the question: interviews for accounts, participant observation for events, audio recording for sound and video for gesture and setting.

Ethics means protecting people and their knowledge. Obtain informed consent: explain the purpose, who will see the material, storage, and the right to withdraw. Recording consent is separate. Follow university ethics review and local permissions. Agree credit, ownership and anonymity; in a small community, names may be identifiable anyway.

sections.heading: In the field
sections.text: Participant observation means taking part in ordinary activities while observing and writing field notes. It helps you learn what people do, not only what they say. Interviews should be open and respectful. Ask clear questions, avoid leading ones, and let silence work. Record only with permission. A useful case is a student studying how a church choir in Lagos learns new songs. She attends rehearsals, interviews singers and the leader, and records with consent. Field notes separate observation from interpretation.

sections.heading: Recording and transcription
sections.text:
Field recording needs good microphones, checked levels, wind protection and backups. Label files with date, place, people and consent status, and store copies in two places. Video adds gesture, dance and setting, but it is more intrusive; discuss where the camera may point.

Transcription turns sound or video into text, notation or time-coded tables. It is selective: no transcript captures everything. Decide whether to mark pitch, rhythm, words, instruments, cues or gestures. Keep original files and a key. Ask a local speaker or musician to check unclear passages.

sections.heading: Analysis and writing
sections.text: Analysis compares transcripts, notes and recordings for patterns, differences and context. Writing up should explain your position and limits (reflexivity), use thick description (detailed context), and avoid speaking for the community. Share drafts with participants (member checking), credit collaborators, and return copies of recordings. The dissertation should show evidence, not only impressions.

keyPoints: Informed consent must cover purpose, storage, access and the right to withdraw, and recording needs separate consent.
Participant observation combines taking part with systematic field notes.
Field recordings need clear labels, consent status and at least two backups.
Transcription is selective; state what you mark and keep a key.
Analysis should connect sounds and statements to context, not just list themes.
Fair representation uses reflexivity, member checking, credit and return of copies.

en.title: Musicology Seminar: Sources, Editing and a Dissertation
en.short: Primary sources, archival and bibliographic method, critical editing, historiography and the master’s dissertation.

sections.heading: Sources and archives
sections.text:
A primary source is a document or object made at the time: a manuscript score, partbook (a book holding one voice part of a set), letter, programme or recording. A secondary source comments on it. Archival method means finding material through catalogues and finding aids, then recording each item consistently: shelfmark (the library’s reference code), date, scribal hand and condition.

Bibliographic method means listing sources fully so another reader can find them. Describe the object as well: paper, watermark, provenance (its ownership history). A church choir book stamped by a missionary tells you about circulation, not only about music.

sections.heading: Editing scores and texts
sections.text:
A critical edition presents a work as accurately as the sources allow. The editor chooses a copy-text, the version used as base, and records variant readings, the differences found in other copies. A stemma, a family tree of copies, shows which copy came from which. The editorial policy states what you correct silently and what you record.

Case: two copies of one partbook differ by a single note. If copy B is a later copy of A, the editor may treat B’s note as an error and list it in the apparatus, the table of variants. If the copies are independent, the editor judges from style and context.

sections.heading: Historiography and argument
sections.text:
Historiography is the study of how history is written: which sources, periods and composers are chosen, and which are left out. Ask who formed the canon, the accepted list of works, and whose music it excludes.

An original argument is a claim others could dispute, supported by evidence and a stated method, and tested against the strongest counterargument. A seminar paper that only summarises sources has no argument.

sections.heading: Planning the dissertation
sections.text: State a research question narrow enough for the word limit. If the dissertation is 15,000 words with four chapters plus a shorter introduction and conclusion, each chapter is about 3,000 words. Keep a source log, agree a chapter plan with your supervisor, and prepare for the defence (viva), if your programme has one, where you explain and defend your claims.

keyPoints: A primary source was made at the time; a secondary source comments on it.
Record shelfmark, date, hand and provenance for every source you consult.
A critical edition names its copy-text and lists variant readings in the apparatus.
Historiography asks who formed the canon and what it leaves out.
An original argument is a disputable claim backed by evidence and method.
Plan chapters to the word limit and prepare to defend your claims at the viva, if your programme has one.
